analysis.one_liner: Caps pain-and-suffering awards in malpractice lawsuits over care paid for by federal health programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in the final weeks of the 109th Congress with zero cosponsors, it was referred to two committees and then a subcommittee, and expired when that Congress ended January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for malpractice lawsuits involving care provided under federal health programs like Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP. It capped compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000, restricted punitive damages, set short deadlines for filing, imposed sanctions on lawyers who file frivolous suits, and let any such case filed in state court be moved to federal court. It left full payment of actual dollar losses — medical bills and lost earnings — untouched, and it barred insurers and benefit programs from taking liens out of a patient's award.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians, hospitals, and drug, device, and biological product makers would gain, because their liability for care provided under Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and EMTALA would be capped at $250,000 for pain and suffering regardless of how severe the injury, and punitive damages would be available only for malicious or deliberately reckless conduct. Malpractice insurers would gain from smaller and more predictable payouts. Ron Paul also framed the bill as protecting taxpayers, on the theory that federal programs absorb the cost of malpractice, though the record here contains only the bill's title and text making that argument.

how_it_helps.text: Caps pain-and-suffering (noneconomic) damages at $250,000 in any lawsuit over health care provided under a federal program, regardless of how many parties or claims are involved.
Lets any such lawsuit filed in state court be moved to federal court, and requires courts to sanction attorneys who file frivolous pleadings, including paying the other side's fees.

Sets strict deadlines — generally 3 years after the injury shows up or 1 year after the patient discovers it — and makes punitive damages available only for malicious or deliberately reckless conduct, capped at the greater of twice economic damages or $250,000.
Bars benefit providers — including insurers and government programs — from taking liens or recovering amounts out of a patient's award, so the patient keeps more of what they win.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by malpractice in care paid for by federal programs would bear the cost: those whose losses are mostly pain and suffering — nursing home residents, children, and disabled people with little lost income — could recover no more than $250,000 no matter how severe the harm. They would also face shorter filing deadlines, possible removal of their cases from state to federal court, and punitive damages nearly out of reach. Trial lawyers handling these cases would face mandatory sanctions for filings deemed frivolous.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients injured under Medicare and Medicaid

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages hits hardest the patients with the smallest economic losses — retirees, children, and disabled people on Medicare and Medicaid — since their compensation depends mostly on noneconomic damages.
The bill would let any health care lawsuit filed in state court be moved to federal court, taking the case away from state courts and the state consumer protections and procedures patients know.

The one-year limit after a patient discovers an injury is short, and mandatory sanctions on attorneys who file pleadings that violate Rule 11 could discourage lawyers from taking legitimate but hard-to-prove cases.

Punitive damages would be available only for conduct proven, by clear and convincing evidence, to be malicious or deliberately reckless, and capped at the greater of twice economic damages or $250,000 — removing the main penalty for the worst corporate misconduct involving medical products.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill was real but contested: supporters argue that malpractice premiums and defensive medicine raise the cost of care, and that federal programs absorb those costs, so capping awards protects taxpayers as well as doctors. The case against it was also substantial: the cap applies exactly where patients are least able to show dollar losses, the one-year discovery window and mandatory sanctions raise the risk that valid claims never get heard, and moving cases to federal court strips away state-law protections. On balance, the bill traded a full remedy for a defined class of injured patients for lower liability costs for providers and manufacturers, with the savings to taxpayers unproven in the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the closing weeks of the 109th Congress, sent to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees and then to a Health subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Ron Paul introduced the bill on September 28, 2006, near the end of the 109th Congress's second session.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee; nothing in the record shows either committee took it up.
On October 2, 2006, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and the record shows no further action of any kind.
No member joined as a cosponsor.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and bills not passed by then die; this one never reached a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients under Medicare and Medicaid are better off, because the bill never came close to passing and they keep the ability to sue in state court for full damages. Physicians, insurers, and medical product makers gained nothing, and taxpayers saw no change in federal program costs either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients who kept full remedies

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 28, 2006 and delivered introductory remarks on it (CR E1904).

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member signed on, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and no organized opposition inside the chamber.

industries.note: Their malpractice exposure for care provided under Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal programs would be capped and moved to federal court. The cost is borne by their injured patients, whose maximum pain-and-suffering recovery would be fixed at $250,000.
Damage caps and shorter deadlines directly limit the payouts that determine malpractice premiums. Patients with large losses absorb the difference.

industries.industry: Drug, device, and biological product makers
industries.note: The bill expressly covers lawsuits against manufacturers, distributors, and sellers of medical products used under federal programs, capping their punitive and noneconomic exposure even for product-related injuries.
Damage caps shrink the contingency fees that make malpractice cases economically viable, and mandatory sanctions raise the risk of taking a hard case. Fewer lawsuits would be filed.
